# Profiling Fortran code

> **Install for this page:** `pip install scope-profiler` supplies the Fortran
> source and requires a Fortran 2008 compiler. For the Python/F2PY example, use
> `pip install "scope-profiler[fortran]"` to add Meson and Ninja.

scope-profiler ships a Fortran module with the same region model as the Python
API. A Fortran program marks regions, writes a small trace file per rank, and
`scope-profiler import-native` turns those traces into the usual HDF5 output —
so a Fortran run gets the same summaries, charts, exporters and `plot`
workflow as a Python one.

The module is deliberately undemanding: plain Fortran 2008 with
`iso_c_binding`, one file, no preprocessor flags, no HDF5, no MPI, nothing to
link beyond libc.

The trace format is shared with {doc}`the C API <c>`, so a program built from
both lands in a single profile.

## Build and run a first profile

The commands below use GNU Fortran on Linux or macOS. Install the Python
package in an activated environment; the compiled Fortran executable itself
needs no Python interpreter. Python is used to locate the module and to
convert and inspect the recorded trace afterwards.

```bash
python -m pip install scope-profiler
sp_source="$(python -c 'from scope_profiler.native_trace import fortran_source_path; print(fortran_source_path())')"
mkdir -p build traces
```

When working from a checkout, use `python -m pip install -e .` instead to
ensure the compiler picks up the local API. You can also copy
`src/scope_profiler/fortran/scope_profiler.f90` into your own project.

Save this complete program as `simulation.f90`. It excludes five warm-up
iterations, measures 100 production iterations, and saves a snapshot every
25 iterations. Replace `solve_system` with your application's work.

```fortran
program simulation
   use scope_profiler
   use, intrinsic :: iso_fortran_env, only: real64, error_unit
   implicit none
   integer :: step, solve, status
   character(len=512) :: message
   type(sp_region_stats) :: stats
   real(real64) :: checksum, total_seconds, mean_seconds

   call sp_init("traces/profile", stat=status, errmsg=message)
   call check_status()
   solve = sp_region("solve", file="simulation.f90", stat=status, errmsg=message)
   call check_status()
   checksum = 0.0_real64

   do step = 1, 5
      call sp_begin(solve)
      call solve_system(checksum)
      call sp_end(solve)
   end do
   call sp_reset(stat=status, errmsg=message) ! same handle, fresh measurements
   call check_status()

   do step = 1, 100
      call sp_begin(solve)
      call solve_system(checksum)
      call sp_end(solve)
      if (mod(step, 25) == 0) then
         call sp_flush(stat=status, errmsg=message)
         call check_status()
      end if
   end do

   call sp_get_region_stats(solve, stats, stat=status, errmsg=message)
   call check_status()
   total_seconds = real(stats%total_ns, real64)*1.0e-9_real64
   mean_seconds = 0.0_real64
   if (stats%calls > 0) mean_seconds = total_seconds/real(stats%calls, real64)
   print *, "completed calls:", stats%calls
   print *, "total / mean seconds:", total_seconds, mean_seconds
   print *, "checksum:", checksum

   call sp_finalize(stat=status, errmsg=message)
   call check_status()

contains

   subroutine solve_system(value)
      real(real64), intent(inout) :: value
      integer :: i
      do i = 1, 10000
         value = value + sqrt(real(i, real64))
      end do
   end subroutine solve_system

   subroutine check_status()
      if (status == SP_OK) return
      write (error_unit, '(a)') trim(message)
      error stop 1
   end subroutine check_status
end program simulation
```

Compile the profiler module first, then compile and link the application:

```bash
gfortran -std=f2008 -O2 -Jbuild -c "$sp_source" -o build/scope_profiler.o
gfortran -std=f2008 -O2 -Ibuild simulation.f90 build/scope_profiler.o -o build/simulation
./build/simulation
python -m scope_profiler import-native traces -o build/profiling_data.h5
python -m scope_profiler inspect build/profiling_data.h5
python -m scope_profiler plot default build/profiling_data.h5 -o build/figures
```

Run these commands from the directory containing `simulation.f90`. The program
writes `traces/profile_rank00000.spt`; its `solve` region should have exactly
100 calls. The checksum includes warm-up work, but the profiling measurements
do not. Keep traces from different runs in different directories so the
importer does not find multiple files claiming the same rank.

### Integrate the module into an existing build

- Compile `scope_profiler.f90` before every source that uses its module.
  With GNU Fortran, `-Jbuild` selects where to write `scope_profiler.mod` and
  `-Ibuild` lets dependent sources find it.
- Link `scope_profiler.o` into the final executable as well as making the
  `.mod` file available during compilation. The `.mod` file alone does not
  contain the implementation.
- Use the same Fortran compiler and compatible options for the profiler and
  its callers. Rebuild the `.mod` file when switching compilers. Other
  compilers may use different module-directory flags.
- Create the output directory before running. `sp_init` stores the output
  prefix; it does not create directories or test whether the file is writable.
  Those failures are reported by `sp_flush` or `sp_finalize`.

The repository also contains ready-made examples:

```bash
# From the repository root, with the package installed in this environment:
make -C examples/fortran run-standalone FC=gfortran PYTHON=python
```

That target compiles the example, runs it, and converts the trace into
`examples/fortran/build/profiling_data.h5`. A smaller `Makefile` and
`example.f90` are also shipped beside the installed profiler module.

## Marking regions

For an existing simulation, place calls around the operations you want to
measure. In this outline, `assemble_matrix` and `solve_system` are your
application routines:

```fortran
program simulation
   use scope_profiler
   implicit none
   integer :: step, solve, assemble

   call sp_init("profile")            ! output prefix

   solve = sp_region("solve")         ! resolve names once...
   assemble = sp_region("assemble")

   do step = 1, 1000
      call sp_begin(assemble)         ! ...then use the handles
      call assemble_matrix()
      call sp_end(assemble)

      call sp_begin(solve)
      call solve_system()
      call sp_end(solve)
   end do

   call sp_finalize()                 ! writes profile_rank00000.spt
end program simulation
```

`sp_begin_name("solve")` / `sp_end_name("solve")` take the name directly, which
reads better in cold code; they look the name up on every call, so prefer the
handle form in hot loops.

Regions may nest, and a region may re-enter itself recursively — each entry
reserves its own slot, exactly as in the Python API.

Nesting must be *proper*: a region entered inside another has to be left
before it. Post-processing reconstructs the call graph from the recorded
intervals, so a `sp_begin`/`sp_end` pair that crosses another region's
boundary — rather than sitting inside or outside it — has no call stack to
recover, and reading the trace back raises `NestingError`. The timings
themselves are still recorded and readable; it is the nesting, the flame
chart and the exclusive times that cannot be derived.

## The API

| Call | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `sp_init(prefix [, rank])` | Start profiling. `rank` (default 0) gives each MPI rank its own trace file. |
| `sp_region(name [, file, line])` | Handle for a region name, with optional source location. |
| `sp_begin(id)` / `sp_end(id)` | Enter and leave a region. |
| `sp_begin_name(name)` / `sp_end_name(name)` | The same, looking the name up each time. |
| `sp_num_calls(id)` | How often a region was entered; readable after `sp_finalize()`. |
| `sp_now_ns()` | The raw clock, in nanoseconds. |
| `sp_is_active()` | Whether profiling is running. |
| `sp_get_region_stats(id, stats)` | Completed-call count and total/minimum/maximum duration in nanoseconds. |
| `sp_flush()` | Write completed calls without stopping or discarding measurements. |
| `sp_reset()` | Clear measurements while preserving handles and source metadata. |
| `sp_finalize()` | Write `<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.spt` and stop. |

### Session lifecycle

Use one initialization per measurement session and resolve handles afterwards.
There is one global profiler per process; independently instrumented libraries
share its region registry and output prefix.

| Operation | What happens to handles and measurements |
| --- | --- |
| `sp_init` | A new session replaces the previous recording. Register handles again. Save the old session first if needed. |
| `sp_flush` | Handles, measurements, and open calls remain valid. Only completed calls appear in the snapshot. |
| `sp_reset` | Handles and source metadata survive; call counts and recorded timings are cleared. All calls must be closed. |
| `sp_finalize` | Recording stops after successful output. Entry counts and completed-call statistics remain readable. |

Before initialization or after finalization, begin/end calls do not record.
Do not cache a handle returned before initialization: `sp_region` returns 0
when inactive. Likewise, a handle from a previous session must be resolved
again after another `sp_init`. Use `sp_is_active()` to check session state.

### Error handling

`sp_init`, `sp_region`, `sp_begin`, `sp_end`, their name-based variants,
`sp_flush`, `sp_reset`, `sp_get_region_stats`, and `sp_finalize` accept
optional `stat=` (default integer) and `errmsg=` (character) outputs.
Success sets `stat` to `SP_OK` and clears `errmsg`. Supplying either output
suppresses stderr diagnostics; without them, errors are reported on stderr.
Instrumentation calls on an inactive profiler remain quiet no-ops, with
`SP_ERR_INACTIVE` returned when requested. Repeated finalization succeeds.

```fortran
integer :: status
character(len=512) :: message

call sp_init("profile", stat=status, errmsg=message)
if (status /= SP_OK) then
   print *, trim(message)
end if
```

Choose a sufficiently long message buffer, such as `character(len=512)`;
Fortran truncates the diagnostic to fit a shorter buffer. Read the outputs
after each call, because the next call overwrites them.

| Status | Meaning and next step |
| --- | --- |
| `SP_OK` | The operation succeeded; `errmsg` is empty. |
| `SP_ERR_INACTIVE` | Initialize before recording, flushing, or resetting. Statistics can still be read after finalization. |
| `SP_ERR_NO_CLOCK` | A supported monotonic clock could not be read. Check platform support; a failed timing call is not a valid measurement. |
| `SP_ERR_NO_MEMORY` | Allocation failed. Existing recordings survive failed growth/flush; reduce recording volume or free memory before retrying. A failed initialization may have replaced the previous session. |
| `SP_ERR_IO` | Check the output directory, permissions, quota, and free space. A failed snapshot may be incomplete; correct the cause and retry output. |
| `SP_ERR_UNMATCHED_END` | Check for an extra end call or a return path that did not enter the region. |
| `SP_ERR_OPEN_SCOPES` | Reset was refused, or finalization saved completed calls while dropping unfinished ones. Close regions before these operations. |
| `SP_ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT` | Check the region handle, prefix length, and rank. |
| `SP_ERR_DEPTH` | The per-region recursion limit was exceeded, or an enclosing entry failed. Its matching end must still be called. |

A failed `sp_region` returns handle 0. Prefixes must contain 1–512
non-trailing-blank characters and ranks must be nonnegative.

`sp_finalize` reports `SP_ERR_OPEN_SCOPES` when it saves completed calls
but drops unfinished calls, including retaining completed recursive children.
On allocation or output failure, flush/finalize retain the measurements and
leave the session active so the application can correct the cause and retry.
Output errors take precedence over unfinished-call diagnostics.

The quick-start program treats profiling failures as fatal for clarity. In a
long-running simulation you may instead log the failure and continue the
calculation. On output failure, retry `sp_flush` or `sp_finalize` after fixing
the cause; calling `sp_init` would replace the measurements you want to save.

Keep begin/end calls paired even when an entry fails for lack of memory,
a clock error, or the recursion limit. A valid region's rejected entry tracks
its matching end so that it cannot accidentally close an outer invocation.
If a region was never registered successfully (handle 0), skip its
instrumentation or register it again before beginning work.

### Snapshots, measurement windows, and statistics

`sp_flush()` writes all completed calls so far to the usual trace path and
continues recording. Open calls are omitted until they finish. Each flush
replaces the previous snapshot; it does not append, clear buffers, or provide
an atomic checkpoint. A failed write may leave an incomplete file. Flush
uses temporary storage of 16 bytes per completed call in the largest region,
in addition to the recording buffers.

`sp_reset()` clears measurements and entry counts while preserving handles,
source locations, and allocated recording capacity. It refuses with
`SP_ERR_OPEN_SCOPES` if any region is open, leaving all measurements intact.
Use it after warm-up or between measurement windows. Reset does not remove
an existing snapshot; the next flush/finalize replaces it.

The complete program at the start of this guide demonstrates this sequence:
reset after warm-up, query statistics, flush periodically, and finalize.

`sp_region_stats` has four `integer(int64)` fields: `calls`, `total_ns`,
`min_ns`, and `max_ns`. These describe completed calls only, use inclusive
durations in nanoseconds, and are all zero when no calls have completed.
Statistics are computed on request by scanning the recorded calls, adding no
running statistics updates to `sp_begin`/`sp_end`. They remain readable after
finalization. In contrast, `sp_num_calls` counts successful entries, including
calls that are still open. Recording buffers are retained after finalization
and released when initialization replaces the session's storage.

For seconds, convert with `real(stats%total_ns, real64)*1.0e-9_real64` after
importing `real64` from `iso_fortran_env`. Compute the mean only when
`stats%calls > 0`, as in the complete example above. Inclusive time contains
work in nested regions, so adding an outer region's total to its children's
totals double-counts that work. Use imported results for call-tree and
exclusive-time analysis.

### Choose snapshot and reset boundaries

For a long run, flush at completed timestep or checkpoint boundaries. Calling
flush while an outer region is open is allowed, but the snapshot omits that
outer call and may show completed children as roots until it closes. Wait
until a flush returns successfully before importing its file, and avoid
reading the path while another flush is replacing it.

Flush retains all measurements, so repeated snapshots are cumulative and do
not bound memory use. Recording uses two growing timestamp arrays per region
(16 bytes per allocated call slot); growth can reserve unused capacity. Reset
lets later calls reuse that capacity but does not shrink it.

For separate measurement windows:

1. Close all regions and call `sp_flush`, checking its status.
2. Copy or convert the snapshot to a separate archive location if you need
   to retain that window. Do this before the next flush replaces it.
3. Call `sp_reset`, checking that it succeeded, then continue using the same
   handles.

Keep archived windows outside the directory passed to `import-native`: files
from separate windows can claim the same rank, and the importer rejects that
ambiguity. For statistics-only progress reports, call `sp_get_region_stats`
at reporting boundaries rather than every iteration; each query scans the
recorded calls.

### Source locations

`sp_region(name, file="solver.f90", line=42)` stores optional source metadata
in the trace and imported HDF5 output. An existing region registered without
a source file can acquire one later. The first nonempty source file wins;
later registrations do not replace its file or line. A missing or negative
line means unknown; a line without a file is ignored. No preprocessing is
required, and cached-handle begin/end calls do not process source metadata.

The file and line are supplied by you; registration does not inspect the
calling source automatically. For example, place this beside the code whose
location you want the profile to identify, and update the line when that
code moves:

```fortran
solve = sp_region("solve", file="src/solver.f90", line=42)
```

Source locations do not distinguish regions with the same name. Use distinct
names such as `fluid:solve` and `particles:solve` when they should have
separate measurements. A relative source path is usually sufficient for
identifying code without embedding a machine-specific absolute path.

## Under MPI

Pass each rank's id so the traces do not collide:

```fortran
call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, my_rank, ierr)
call sp_init("profile", rank=my_rank)
```

Every rank writes its own file; nothing is communicated, so `sp_finalize()` is
not collective and a rank that dies takes only its own trace with it. The
importer merges whatever it finds. Create the shared output directory before
launching, and initialize the profiler after `MPI_Init`/`MPI_Comm_rank`.
Finalize the profiler on each rank before `MPI_Finalize`. The profiler itself
makes no MPI calls, and flushing one rank does not wait for others.

Use your MPI compiler wrapper to build the application and the profiler with
the same underlying compiler. After compiling your MPI-aware `simulation`,
run it from a fresh trace directory:

```bash
mkdir -p mpi-run
(cd mpi-run && mpirun -n 128 ../simulation)
python -m scope_profiler import-native mpi-run -o mpi-run/profiling_data.h5
python -m scope_profiler plot default mpi-run/profiling_data.h5 -o mpi-run/figures
```

## From Python

```python
from scope_profiler.native_trace import load_traces, convert_traces

results = load_traces("run_dir")            # -> ProfilingResults, as usual
results.print_summary()
results.to_dataframe()

convert_traces("run_dir", "profiling_data.h5", label="128 ranks")
```

`load_traces` returns the very same `ProfilingResults` a Python run produces,
so every method, `plot_*` function and exporter works on it unchanged.

## One timeline with Python

The module reads the same OS clock CPython's `time.perf_counter_ns()` uses —
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux, `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW` on macOS — and picks it by
probing at run time rather than by compile-time platform macros, which
gfortran does not reliably define.

That means Fortran and Python regions recorded in the same process tree share
an epoch: a Python driver's timestamps and its Fortran kernels' timestamps are
directly comparable, and can be read on one timeline.

## Python calling Fortran

The case this is really for: a Python driver over Fortran kernels, where both
sides mark regions and you want **one** profile. Because the two APIs read the
same clock, their timestamps are directly comparable — the Fortran regions nest
inside the Python region that called them, and `call_stack()` sees a single
tree spanning both languages.

Compile `scope_profiler.f90` alongside the kernels using f2py, ctypes,
Cython, or your existing extension build. With f2py, restrict Python wrappers
using `only:` to your kernel entry points. The profiler's derived types and
named integer kinds are intended for Fortran callers, not direct f2py
wrapping. Expose wrappers for initialization and finalization alongside the
computational routines.

For example, this complete kernel module can be saved as `kernels.f90`:

```fortran
module kernels
   use scope_profiler
   implicit none
   integer :: solve_id = 0
contains
   subroutine start_profiling(prefix, rank)
      character(len=*), intent(in) :: prefix
      integer, intent(in) :: rank
      call sp_init(prefix, rank=rank)
      solve_id = sp_region("fortran:solve", file="kernels.f90")
   end subroutine start_profiling

   subroutine stop_profiling()
      call sp_finalize()
   end subroutine stop_profiling

   subroutine solve(n, value)
      integer, intent(in) :: n
      double precision, intent(out) :: value
      integer :: i
      call sp_begin(solve_id)
      value = 0.0d0
      do i = 1, n
         value = value + sqrt(dble(i))
      end do
      call sp_end(solve_id)
   end subroutine solve
end module kernels
```

Build it from the directory containing `kernels.f90`:

```bash
python -m pip install "scope-profiler[fortran]"
sp_source="$(python -c 'from scope_profiler.native_trace import fortran_source_path; print(fortran_source_path())')"
python -m numpy.f2py -c "$sp_source" kernels.f90 -m kernels --backend meson \
  only: start_profiling stop_profiling solve :
```

Keep `meson` and `ninja` on `PATH` by activating the environment where the
Fortran extra is installed. Then save this as `run_mixed.py` beside the built
extension and run it with `python run_mixed.py`. `finalize()` folds the
Fortran trace into the Python result:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import kernels
from scope_profiler import ProfileManager

Path("mixed-traces").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
ProfileManager.setup(file_path="mixed_profile.h5")
kernels.kernels.start_profiling("mixed-traces/trace", 0)  # serial rank

for step in range(3):
    with ProfileManager.region("python:step"):
        value = kernels.kernels.solve(10000)

kernels.kernels.stop_profiling()
ProfileManager.finalize(native_traces="mixed-traces")
```

The resulting `mixed_profile.h5` contains three `python:step` calls and three
`fortran:solve` calls nested inside them. Inspect it with
`python -m scope_profiler inspect mixed_profile.h5`. The repository's
`examples/fortran` directory has a larger example; run it with
`make -C examples/fortran run-mixed PYTHON=python` from the repository root.

Two rules:

- **Call the Fortran `sp_finalize()` first.** Its trace has to exist by the
  time `finalize()` reads it.
- **Give the two sides distinct region names.** A name recorded by both raises,
  rather than silently double-counting a wrapper and the region inside it. A
  `python:` / `fortran:` prefix is the simplest convention.

Under MPI each rank folds in the trace matching its own rank, so pass the rank
to `sp_init` and nothing else changes — the usual single output file comes out
the other end.

### Combining afterwards

If the two halves were profiled separately, merge them after the fact:

```bash
scope-profiler import-native traces/ --merge python_only.h5 -o combined.h5
```

or in Python:

```python
from scope_profiler import merge_results, read_h5
from scope_profiler.native_trace import load_traces

combined = merge_results(read_h5("python_only.h5"), load_traces("traces/"))
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Compiler cannot find `scope_profiler.mod` | Compile the profiler first; point the caller's module search path at its output directory. |
| Linker reports undefined profiler symbols | Link the profiler object, built with the same compiler as the caller. |
| No trace exists after initialization | Output is written by flush/finalize, not init. Check their status and the process's working directory. |
| Trace file exists but is truncated | Output may have failed. Check status, fix the cause, and retry from the still-active session. |
| Snapshot has fewer calls than `sp_num_calls` | Entry counts include open calls; snapshots and statistics include completed calls only. |
| Reset reports open regions | Match every begin with an end, including on early returns, before resetting. |
| Imported call graph raises `NestingError` | Check properly nested begin/end pairs and avoid simultaneous instrumentation from multiple OpenMP threads. |
| Import reports duplicate ranks | Use one trace per rank per run directory. Keep archived snapshots and previous runs elsewhere. |
| f2py build cannot find Meson/Ninja | Activate the environment containing `scope-profiler[fortran]` so its tools are on `PATH`. |
| f2py tries to wrap profiler types or kinds | Restrict wrappers with `only:` to the kernel routines called by Python. |

## The trace format

`sp_finalize()` writes `<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.spt`, a small binary file:

```
char[8]   "SCOPEPRF"
int32     format version (2)
int32     rank
int64     number of regions
per region:
    int32     length of the name in bytes
    char[]    name
    int32     length of source file in bytes (0 if unknown)
    char[]    source file
    int32     source line (-1 if unknown)
    int64     number of calls
    int64[]   start timestamps, nanoseconds
    int64[]   end timestamps, nanoseconds
```

Native endianness; the reader detects and handles both. 16 bytes per recorded
call, the same as the Python side.

The reader also accepts legacy version-1 traces without source locations.

## Limitations

- **Not thread safe.** A region must be entered and left by the same thread.
  OpenMP threads inside a region are fine — wrap the whole parallel construct
  in one `sp_begin`/`sp_end` from the master thread.
- **No LIKWID counters.** Hardware counters are collected only by the Python
  API; a Fortran trace carries timings alone.
- **Names are truncated** at `SP_MAX_NAME` (128) characters, including for
  lookup. Names sharing those first 128 characters refer to the same region.
- **Recursion depth** per region is capped at `SP_MAX_DEPTH` (64); deeper
  entries return `SP_ERR_DEPTH` and are not timed. Their matching ends are
  consumed without closing an outer call.
- **A region still open at `sp_finalize()`** is omitted from the trace and
  reported with `SP_ERR_OPEN_SCOPES`. Completed recursive children are kept.
